title: Script Family Tree
description: A simplified family tree of South Asian scripts. Brahmi branches through the Gupta, Sharada, Nagari, Gaudi, Kadamba and Pallava scripts to Gurmukhi, Devanagari, Gujarati, Bengali-Assamese, Odia, Tibetan, Kannada, Telugu, Tamil, Malayalam and Sinhala. A second root, Aramaic, leads to Kharoshthi and, through Arabic, to the Perso-Arabic script and Thaana. Learners click a script to see how it writes ka, ki, ku and a bare k in real Unicode characters, and which languages use it.
creator: Aaryav Sharma

publisher: Roots & Rivers: An Interactive Guide to South Asian Cultures for High School Students
audience: Students, Educators, South Asian student club leaders
learningObjectives: Explain that many South Asian scripts share Brahmi as a common ancestor.
Explain how an abugida writes a consonant with an inherent vowel that vowel marks can change or remove.
Distinguish scripts of the Brahmi family from the Perso-Arabic script and Thaana.
prerequisites: Knowing that a script (a way of writing) and a language (a way of speaking) are different things
Knowing what consonants and vowels are
keyQuestions: Why do Bangla, Hindi, Punjabi and Tamil letters look so different if their scripts are related?
How does one base letter become ka, ki, ku or a bare k in an abugida?
Which South Asian scripts do not come from Brahmi?
misconceptions: A script and a language are the same thing.
Scripts that look different cannot be related.
Hindi and Urdu are unrelated because they use different scripts.
Dravidian languages such as Tamil and Telugu must use a script unrelated to Hindi's.
controls: Sound menu (ka, ki, ku, k with no vowel)
